title: Semantic HTML
subtitle: Transform your webpage into professional production code
description: Learn semantic elements header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer, time, address - turn your div-soup into meaningful structure that Google ranks higher and screen readers love. This is what separates junior webpages from professional complete webpages.

blocks.text: Your webpage works but is it professional? Let's find out

So far your webpage uses div, h1, p, ul - it works visually. But open any big company website's code - you won't see 100 divs. You will see header, nav, main, section, article, footer. Why? Because div means nothing - it's generic container. Semantic elements mean something - they tell browser, Google and screen readers what that part IS. Today we refactor your complete webpage to professional standard.
Open Menu > Practical and open your index.html from Lesson 6. We are going to rewrite it semantically - same look, but 10x more professional underneath.
Why semantics decides if your webpage ranks on Google

Semantic HTML is HTML that conveys meaning, not just presentation. div and span are non-semantic - they tell nothing about content. header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer, time, mark, figure are semantic - they define role. Benefits: 1) SEO - Google understands your webpage structure better and ranks higher. 2) Accessibility - screen readers announce landmarks like 'navigation', 'main', 'complementary'. 3) Maintainability - other developers understand your webpage in seconds.

blocks.text: The 7 layout elements that build every complete webpage

Every professional webpage uses this structure: header = top intro with logo and nav, nav = navigation links (can be inside header or separate), main = main content of this page - only ONE per page, section = thematic grouping like About section, Services section, article = independent content that could stand alone like blog post or project card, aside = related but secondary content like sidebar, footer = bottom with copyright, links.

blocks.text: Section vs Article vs Div - when to use which

This confuses even intermediate devs. Rule: section = thematic grouping of content, usually with heading, groups related content. article = independent, self-contained content that would make sense alone if shared - blog post, project card, news article, comment. div = generic container with no semantic meaning, use only when no semantic element fits, or for styling wrapper. If you can remove div and structure still makes sense, you probably don't need div.

blocks.text: Main must be unique - critical rule

You must have only ONE main per page, and it must contain main content of that page - not header, not footer, not sidebar. Also main should not be inside header, footer, nav, article, aside. This helps screen readers jump directly to main content with shortcut. Many beginners put multiple mains or wrap whole page in main including header/footer - that's invalid.

options: No improvement, div and header/nav are identical for SEO and accessibility, semantic tags are just shorter to type

Improves because header and nav provide landmark semantics - search engines understand page structure and rank sections better, screen readers announce landmarks allowing blind users to jump to navigation/main instantly, while div has no semantic meaning and is ignored as generic container

blocks.question: You have webpage with list of 3 projects. Each project has title, image, description, link. Should each project be section or article and why?
options: section because projects are sections of portfolio page, article is only for blog posts not for projects

article because each project is independent, self-contained content that could be syndicated/shared alone and makes sense on its own, while section is thematic grouping - so projects section contains multiple project articles
div because projects are just divs with styling, article and section are deprecated and should not be used for projects
main because each project is main content of page, so each project should be main element
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Section groups theme, article is independent piece. Portfolio: Projects section contains Project articles.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Could you share one project card alone on social media and would it still make sense? That's article test.
blocks.reasoning: article = independent, self-contained, distributable. section = thematic grouping. Projects list: section#projects groups theme, each project is article.

blocks.question: You add two <main> elements - one for About, one for Projects - to make styling easier. Validator says error. What is rule for main and correct fix?
options: main can be used multiple times, validator is wrong, multiple mains are allowed in HTML5 for different topics

Rule is only one main per page, main must contain main content of document, not include header/footer/nav, and must not be descendant of those. Fix: One main wrapping all main sections like About, Projects, Contact
Rule is main must be inside header, so move both mains inside header to fix error
Rule is main must have id attribute, add id="main1" and id="main2" to fix multiple mains error
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! One main per page is critical rule for accessibility landmarks.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: How many main contents does a page have? Can you have two main contents?
blocks.reasoning: Spec: Only one visible main per page, unique main content, not inside header/footer/nav/article/aside. Multiple mains break landmark navigation.

blocks.title: Semantic checklist for your final webpage
blocks.code:
<!-- Checklist for your complete webpage -->
<header> - One, top, contains h1 and nav
<nav> - For navigation links, can be in header or separate
<main> - One only, contains main content, not header/footer
<section> - Thematic groups, must have heading h2/h3, groups related content
<article> - Independent content that could stand alone - project cards, blog posts
<aside> - Secondary content like sidebar, related links
<footer> - Bottom, copyright, secondary nav
<figure> + <figcaption> - For images with captions
<time datetime=""> - Machine-readable dates for SEO
<address> - Contact info for article or page
<mark> - Highlighted text
blocks.output: Use this checklist to audit your webpage before Lesson 10 submission

blocks.question: You have <section> without heading and <div> wrapping single paragraph that could be section. Which is correct usage and why does section need heading?
options: Both are fine, section doesn't need heading and div can replace section anywhere with no semantic loss

section should have heading h2-h6 because section is thematic grouping and heading defines its theme for outline, search engines and screen readers. If no heading needed and it's just styling wrapper, use div instead of section. div has no semantic requirement
section must always contain article, not just paragraph, so wrap paragraph in article inside section to be valid
div is semantic and section is non-semantic, so use div for important content and section for decorative wrappers
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Section = thematic grouping with heading. No heading? Probably div.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: What defines theme of a section? How does outline algorithm know theme?
blocks.reasoning: Section represents thematic grouping, should have heading to define theme. Without heading, use div as generic container.

blocks.question: You place <address> inside <footer> with your email and physical address for entire site. Also you use <time datetime="2026-05-11">May 11</time> for blog post date. Are both correct semantic uses?
options: Both incorrect: address should be inside header not footer, and time should be inside footer not article

Both correct: address in footer for site-wide contact is valid - address represents contact info for its nearest article or body ancestor, footer address means site contact; time with datetime provides machine-readable date for SEO and is correct for publish dates
address correct but time incorrect because time must have only date without datetime attribute, datetime is deprecated
time correct but address incorrect because address can only contain email not physical address
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect semantic understanding! address scope and time datetime are production details.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: What does address represent? Contact for nearest ancestor. What does datetime provide?
blocks.reasoning: address = contact info for nearest article/body ancestor. In footer, it's site contact. time datetime = machine-readable for SEO, human-readable content can be different format.
